title: How this book works
lead: A London street cry: bakers sang it to sell hot spiced buns on Good Friday.
time_html:
Count 1 2 in every bar, steady as a clock: two beats a bar.

Walk on a beat; run two quick notes in one beat: say pen-ny, count 1 +.
pos:
Your hand. Right hand: finger 2 on middle C, 3 on D, 4 on E: the three middle fingers.

Steps down. E, D, C: each note is the next key down, and on the page each sits a step lower.
sing_how: Listen, pointing to each note. Sing it with the words, then on the letter names.
names_how: Now the notes are empty. Write E, D or C in each box, then sing it on the letter names.
more_how: The same three keys, a new way: a robot that walks with the band. Then make a tune of your own.
wow: Your first song with a band. Three notes, and you are already playing with drums and bass: scan the code, choose the band, and play on top. Then open your passport: Lesson 1 issues it.
trick: One note here is wrong. Play it, then the same bars on page 1: which note sounds wrong? Circle it.

yours.how: Pick one and play the whole song that way. Record it on a phone and listen back: does it sound the way you meant?
pick: Robot: every note short and stiff
Giant: slow and heavy, big footsteps

menu: As a giant, then a mouse
rhy_how: Say the words in time, then clap and count: clap on the coral numbers, hold through the grey ones.
label: Start here

gig.job: Welcome to Music Box 2. Two new things today. The letters now sit inside the notes. And the left hand plays its first whole chord: three keys at once.
gig.tool_how: Left hand. On C, play C; on G, play G. Once, on beat 1, and let it ring to the end of the bar.
gig.tool_cap: The C chord: C, E and G together, fingers 5, 3 and 1. F alone with finger 2. G alone with the thumb.
gig.song_how: A black note lasts one box. A white note with a stem lasts two. A white note with no stem fills the whole bar. Press the chord on beat 1 and hold it down.
gig.real: Play it for someone younger. Count them in, 1 2 3 4, and do not stop.
gig.r_cap: Thumb on middle C. A is one key past your little finger: reach for it, then come back.
gig.ready: all three keys of the C chord go down at the same moment.
ways_txt: Play the chord again on beat 3: twice in a bar instead of once.
Move the right hand up to the next C: the same keys, eight keys higher. Baby ducks.

Music Box 2

Thirteen songs and one old friend

In Music Box 1 you played from letters in boxes. In this book the letters slowly turn into real notes, and the left hand grows from one key into whole chords that move. One new thing in each song, never two. The last page is Twinkle again: same tune, new left hand, so you can hear how far you have come.

How to use this book

For anyone learning without a teacher, and for teachers too

Two pages for every song

The left page gets you ready: the one new thing, where each hand sits, how to read the page, and five steps to practise in order. The right page is the song. Do not skip the left page.

How fast to go

About one song a week. Ten minutes every day is worth more than an hour on Sunday. Each right page ends with Ready for the next song when. When that line is true and the four boxes are ticked, turn the page. If not, stay: nothing is lost by staying.

If you get stuck
  1. Play at half the speed. Then half of that.
  2. Take one line a day, not the whole song.
  3. Go back one song and play it once for pleasure. It will feel easy now: that is what progress feels like.
What the signs mean
  • Numbers above the notes: fingers. 1 is the thumb, 5 the little finger, in both hands.
  • Numbers below the notes: the count. Say it out loud.
  • A black note lasts one box. A white note with a stem lasts two. A white note with no stem fills a bar of four.
  • A dot after a note makes it half as long again. The short note after it comes late, on and.
  • Notes joined by a beam are quick: two of them share one box.
  • ♯ before a note: the black key just to its right. ♭: the black key just to its left.
  • An arrow ↑ or ↓: the higher or the lower key of that name.
  • Coral letters over the left hand: the name of the chord. m means minor, the darker kind.
  • Letters stacked in a box: play those keys together.
  • A long line after a note or chord: keep holding.
For teachers

Each song adds exactly one thing; the table on the first page names it. The left-hand patterns are the standard ways to accompany a melody, in order: whole chord, changing chord, split chord, broken chord, an independent line, a ground bass. The last box on each left page turns the song into a small arranging exercise.

Where the tunes come from

Every melody in this book was checked note by note against an open score

All fourteen tunes are old enough to belong to everyone. Each was compared, pitch by pitch and length by length, with a published open edition. Where this book differs, the last column says how.

SongChecked againstWhat is different here
1All My Little Ducklings
Traditional, Germany		Essen folk-song collection (Alle meine Entchen)As in the source.
2Oh! Susanna
Stephen Foster, 1848		Nottingham Music Database (Oh Susanna)In the chorus the long A is written as it is sung; the source, a dance version, repeats it.
3Little Brown Jug
Joseph Winner, 1869		Nottingham Music Database (Little Brown Jug)Two lead-in notes that fiddlers add between the halves are left out.
4Deck the Halls
Traditional, Wales		Nottingham Music Database (Nos Galan), bars 1 to 12Lines 1 to 3 are the source. Line 4 is the ending everyone sings, which the dance version does not write out.
5The First Noel
Traditional, England		Mutopia Project (The First Noel, soprano)Verse once, then the refrain.
6Good King Wenceslas
Tune from 1582; words J. M. Neale, 1853		Nottingham Music Database (GKW); Mutopia ProjectAs in the sources. Line 1 is played twice.
7Silent Night
Franz Gruber, 1818		Mutopia Project (Stille Nacht, soprano); Essen folk-song collectionAs in the Mutopia score.
8Daisy Bell
Harry Dacre, 1892		Nottingham Music Database (Daisy Daisy), first halfFirst half of the chorus. One lead-in note that is not sung is left out.
9Minuet in G
Christian Petzold, in Anna Magdalena Bach’s notebook		Mutopia Project (BWV Anh. 114), bars 1 to 16, both handsBoth hands as written.
10Greensleeves
Traditional, England, 1500s		Mutopia Project (Greensleeves, soprano), first half, moved from E minor to A minorFirst half.
11Canon
Johann Pachelbel, late 1600s		Mutopia Project (Canon per 3 violini e basso), bars 3 to 7, moved from D to CThe first two phrases of the first violin and the start of the third, then a closing C. The bass as written.
12In the Hall of the Mountain King
Edvard Grieg, 1875		Mutopia Project (Grieg, Op. 46 No. 4), bars 2 to 5, moved from B minor to A minorThe four-bar theme, with its bass.
13Für Elise
Ludwig van Beethoven, 1810		Mutopia Project (Beethoven, WoO 59), bars 1 to 8The first eight bars, both hands as written.
Twinkle, Now
Traditional, France, 1700s		Traditional tune (Ah! vous dirai-je, maman), as in Music Box 1The tune as in Music Box 1; the chords are ours.

Some tunes are moved to a key that sits under the hand; the notes keep their distances. The left-hand chords and all the fingerings are this book’s own. Open scores: Mutopia Project (mutopiaproject.org), Nottingham Music Database, Essen Folksong Collection.
